Rosenberg’s diaries from the years 1934 to 1944 were believed to have disappeared after 1945. In fact, Robert Kempner had possession of the manuscript and took it with him to the United States. It was not rediscovered until 2013 and was published in 2015: A. Rosenberg, Die Tagebücher von 1934 bis 1944, ed. Jürgen Matthäus and Frank Bajohr, Frankfurt am Main 2015.
the Hochland high up in Bavaria — Refers to the journal Hochland, published in Munich. It was banned in 1941 and re-established in November 1946.
Maxime Leroy — (1873–1957), French lawyer and social historian; M. Leroy, La vie véritable du Comte Henri de Saint-Simon (1760–1825), Paris 1925. The following quotation is on p. 222.

in the presence of Mr. Friesenhahn — Ernst Friesenhahn (1901–1984) had been Schmitt’s assistant at the University of Bonn from 1925 onward and received his doctorate under Schmitt in 1928. Their relationship broke down because of Schmitt’s involvement with National Socialism. From 1947 to 1948 Friesenhahn served as dean of the Faculty of Law and Political Science at the University of Bonn.
Kirchheimer — Otto Kirchheimer (1905–1965), a student of Schmitt who, like Friesenhahn, received his doctorate under Schmitt in 1928; see BW Forsthoff, p. 360.
Reinach, Durkheim — Salomon Reinach (1858–1932), French art historian and scholar of religion. Émile Durkheim (1858–1917), French sociologist and ethnologist.

Reading Rudolf Diels — Rudolf Diels (1900–1957) entered the Prussian police service in 1930 and worked with Papen and Schleicher in 1932. Schmitt had known him since that time. When the Gestapa—the Prussian Secret State Police Office—was created, Diels became its first chief, but he was removed from the post by the end of 1933. He then went on to have a varied and ambiguous career under the Nazi regime, while also maintaining contacts with the resistance. After 1945 he worked for the American military government and appeared as a witness at the Nuremberg trials.

In his autobiography, Diels describes meeting Schmitt in Nuremberg just after Schmitt had been released from detention. Schmitt greeted him with Hutten’s exclamation: “It is a joy to be alive.” Rudolf Diels, Lucifer ante portas. Zwischen Severing und Heydrich, Zurich [1949], p. 322.

as he appears in Shakespeare — In the note cited above (Leviathan, p. 40), Schmitt refers to Henry V, Act 3, Scene 3; A Midsummer Night’s Dream, Act 2, Scene 1; and The Two Gentlemen of Verona, Act 3, Scene 2.

aeque enim transgredientes aequaliter puniri jubet aequitas naturalis — Thomas Hobbes, De cive, XIII.16. “For natural equity requires that those who break a law be punished equally.” Hobbes, M/B, p. 215.

the fate of Miorița — A popular Romanian ballad. Three shepherds meet with their flocks. One of the sheep, named Miorița, tells its shepherd that the other shepherds are going to kill him. The shepherd then addresses the animal and says that, when he dies, he wants to be buried beside his sheep.

Automatic < Arrest > — After the end of the war in 1945, the Allies placed political officials of the Nazi state under “automatic arrest.” Schmitt did not belong to the category of people covered by this policy, so his detention in 1945–46 was not, contrary to his repeated claims, an “automatic arrest.” See Quaritsch in Carl Schmitt – Antworten in Nürnberg, edited and annotated by Helmut Quaritsch, Berlin 2000, pp. 11–12.

Aroneanu — Eugène Aroneanu (?–1960), jurist and Romanian resistance fighter. He emigrated to Paris in the 1930s, then to Switzerland in 1943, and prepared a list of Nazi war crimes for the Nuremberg trials. Schmitt is referring to Eugène Aroneanu, Das Verbrechen gegen die Menschlichkeit (excerpt from the Nouvelle Revue de droit internationale privé, no. 2, 1946), Baden-Baden 1947.
the figure of Scaeva — Schmitt is referring to Pharsalia, Book VI, where Scaeva turns against his own troops.
the Biedenhorns — Biedenhorn is a character in Ernst Jünger’s story On the Marble Cliffs: a mercenary commander who conducts himself with tactical skill during a civil war.

Compare my essay on Vitoria — Published anonymously: [C. Schmitt], “Francisco de Vitoria und die Geschichte seines Ruhmes,” in Die neue Ordnung 3 (1949), pp. 289–313. The essay was based on lectures delivered in Spain and Portugal in 1944 and was later included in Nomos, pp. 69–96.
Malraux — André Malraux (1910–1976), French existentialist writer and politician. His early novels deal with the human condition in revolution and civil war.
minor vobis causae vestrae amor quam mihi mortis — Correctly:
Pompei vobis minor est causaeque senatus / Quam mihi mortis amor.
“Pompey’s cause and the Senate’s mean less to you than death means to me.” Pharsalia, VI, 245–46.

Nos actes nous suivent — “Our actions follow us.” Schmitt is probably referring to Revelation 14:13. He may also have had in mind the novel of the same title by the French Catholic writer Paul Bourget (1852–1935), published in Paris in 1927.
Non omnis moriar — “I shall not wholly die.” Horace, Carmina III.30.6.
Veit Valentin is right — Schmitt is referring to V. Valentin, Geschichte der Deutschen, Berlin 1947.

excommunication of Communism — A decree of the Holy Office dated 1 July 1949, dealing with the attitude Catholics were to take toward the Communist Party, declared Catholic faith and Communism incompatible. See Acta Apostolicae Sedis 41 (1949), pp. 333–334; German translation in Herder-Korrespondenz 3 (1949), no. 11, p. 487.

liberation from the dreadful Cauchemaritain — A blend of cauchemar (“nightmare”) and “Maritain,” meaning Jacques Maritain. Maritain, who was accused by some of sympathizing with Communism, served as French ambassador to the Vatican from 1945 to 1948. His idea of “Integral Humanism” influenced the social teaching of Pope Pius XII. Schmitt apparently hoped that the decree would put an end to this influence.

the return of Herr Hausenstein — Wilhelm Hausenstein (1882–1957), German cultural historian, writer, and diplomat. Schmitt had already met him in Munich in 1915; see Tb 1915. In 1950, Hausenstein was sent to Paris by the West German government, first as consul general and then as the Federal Republic’s first German ambassador there.

Hans Peters — (1896–1966), constitutional lawyer and CDU politician. After 1945 he was one of the leading figures opposing Schmitt’s return to university teaching. See his report of 17 June 1946, Humboldt University of Berlin, University Archive, Faculty of Law, no. 524, fols. 5–6. He also opposed Schmitt’s admission to the Association of German Constitutional Law Teachers. See Levin von Trott zu Solz, Hans Peters und der Kreisauer Kreis. Staatslehre im Widerstand, Paderborn et al., 1997.
as possessions lost, fermented into time — From a dedicatory poem for Carl Schmitt by Konrad Weiß:
“Our possessions are lost to us, fermented into the world we share.”
Omnis actio humana specificatur ex objecto — Correctly:
actus omnis habet speciem ab obiecto; et actus humanus, qui dicitur moralis, habet speciem ab obiecto relato ad principium actuum humanorum, quod est ratio.
“Every act takes its character from its object; and a human act, which is called moral, takes its character from the object as related to the principle of human action, namely reason.”
Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae, I–II, q. 18, a. 8, c.

Sicilian Vespers — The name given to the uprising against the French occupation in Palermo on 30 March 1282. To stop disguised French soldiers from escaping, people were made to pronounce the words “cece, cici, ciceri.”

Hans Berger — (1909–1985), jurist and diplomat. At the time he was president of the Düsseldorf Regional Court. From 1954 onward he served in the diplomatic service of the Federal Republic of Germany and, beginning in 1959, as ambassador to various countries. He was also, for a period, head of the Office of the Federal President.
Language is the house of Being. — Quotation from Martin Heidegger’s “Letter on Humanism.”
sustained by the inner image that cannot be possessed — An allusion to Konrad Weiß’s poem “Justitia,” dedicated to Carl Schmitt, which begins:
“In that confused age, the law no longer bent itself toward the inner image.”

Jellinek — “Law, then, as the preserving element, will form the minimum of norms required by a particular state of society; in other words, it will include those norms that guarantee the continued existence of that society without fundamental change.” Georg Jellinek, Die sozialethische Bedeutung von Recht, Unrecht und Strafe, 2nd ed., Berlin 1908, p. 45.
Grote — Manfred Grote, political scientist. In 1962 he wrote “Political ideas of Carl Schmitt and the ‘Nihilism of the 20th century’” (MA thesis, University of Kansas).
numquid et vos vultis abire? — “Do you also want to leave?” Vulgate, John 6:68; Luther Bible, John 6:67.

the Roman Church as a ghost — “And if a man considers the origin of this great ecclesiastical dominion, he will easily see that the Papacy is nothing other than the ghost of the deceased Roman Empire, sitting crowned upon its grave.” Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, trans. Jutta Schlösser, ed. Hermann Klenner, Hamburg 1996, p. 586.

Lenin’s ideal was the electrified earth — Schmitt quoting himself: “The great entrepreneur has no ideal other than Lenin’s, namely an ‘electrified earth.’” RK, p. 22; see also FoP, pp. 846–47, with note 24 on p. 861.

When someone suffers a defeat … — Schmitt is referring to the essay “Darf ein Mensch für die Wahrheit sich totschlagen lassen?” in the following edition: Søren Kierkegaard, Der Begriff des Auserwählten, translation and afterword by Theodor Haecker, Hellerau 1917; Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 24274.

“For when someone suffers a defeat, you do not fully see how weak he is; you see how strong the other man is. But when someone wins and then collapses helplessly, you see how weak he is and always was—and how strong the other man was: the man who tricked him into winning in such a way, who tricked him into being shattered by victory as no defeat could ever have shattered him.”
Regnare enim dicitur non qui agendo … — “For we say that a man rules when he governs not through his actions but through his words, that is, through commands and threats.” Hobbes, M/B, p. 236.
proprie et accurate loquendo — “in the proper and exact meaning of the word”; the phrase belongs to the longer Hobbes quotation.
Rheema; rheemasin peithomenoi … — Rheema (ῥῆμα) means “command.” Schmitt is alluding to the famous epigram by Simonides of Ceos:
Ὦ ξεῖν’, ἀγγέλλειν Λακεδαιμονίοις, ὅτι τῇδε κείμεθα, τοῖς κείνων ῥήμασι πειθόμενοι.
“Wanderer, if you come to Sparta, tell them there that you saw us lying here, as the law commanded.”
The best thing in the world is a command — See LuL, p. 13. Schmitt is freely translating Hobbes:
Tertio, quod imperare et imperata intelligere possimus, beneficium sermonis est, et quidem maximum.
“Third, that we are able to command and to understand commands is a benefit of language—and indeed its greatest benefit.”
Thomas Hobbes, Opera philosophica, ed. G. Molesworth, vol. II, London 1889, p. 91.
Schmoller — Gustav von Schmoller (1907–1991), diplomat, formerly Schmitt’s doctoral student and assistant at Berlin University.
a fine gloss of mine — st [= C. Schmitt], “Maritime Weltpolitik,” in Christ und Welt, 6 October 1949. Reprinted in SGN, pp. 478–480.
Christinform — See Erich Schieweck, Christinform oder Kominform, das kommende Deutschland, Hamburg 1949.

von der Heydte — Friedrich August von der Heydte (1907–1994), constitutional lawyer, soldier, and politician. The “desecration of asylum” refers to von der Heydte’s “reply” to Schmitt’s “Francisco de Vitoria und die Geschichte seines Ruhms,” published in Die Friedenswarte 49 (1949), pp. 190–197.
See also Schmitt to Forsthoff, 1 December 1949, in BW Forsthoff, pp. 59–60, and to E. R. Huber, 10 December 1949, in BW Huber, pp. 352 ff.
Klaus Mehnert — (1906–1984), political journalist and commentator.
Welty — Eberhard Welty (1902–1965), prior of the Dominican monastery at Walberberg. During these years he gave Schmitt opportunities to publish in the journal Die neue Ordnung, which Welty edited.

How beautiful and gratifying successful rhymes are — In 1950, Schmitt told Nicolaus Sombart that he wanted to write an essay about rhyme (BW Sombart, p. 36). He never did, but material for it survives among his papers: RW 265 no. 20801.
Ernst Jünger’s miserable voice — At the beginning of November 1949, Jünger visited Schmitt. Anima Schmitt wrote about the visit to her mother on 7 November 1949:
“…Peter Heinrich, being a musical person, interpreted him [Jünger] entirely through his voice and shuddered at the thought of seeing his larynx.”
In Gerd Giesler, Carl Schmitt und die Künste der Plettenberger Nachkriegszeit (Plettenberger Miniaturen, 3), Plettenberg 2010, p. 26.

Herr Jaspers’s … bacillophobia — Schmitt knew the expression “bacillophobia” through Gerhard Nebel. Jaspers had used it in conversation with Nebel, who reported this in a letter to Schmitt dated 7 October 1949 (RW 265 no. 10170).
